'''Gerard Kitchen O'Neill''' (February 6, 1927 – April 27, 1992) was an American [[physicist]] and [[Space advocacy|space activist]]. As a faculty member of [[Princeton University]], he invented a device called the [[Storage ring|particle storage ring]] for high-energy physics experiments.<ref name="physrev-sr" /> Later, he invented a magnetic launcher called the [[mass driver]].<ref>{{harvnb|Dyson|1993|pp=97–98}}</ref> In the 1970s, he developed a plan to build human settlements in outer space, including a [[space habitat]] design known as the [[O'Neill cylinder]]. He founded the [[Space Studies Institute]], an organization devoted to funding research into [[space manufacturing]] and [[Space colonization|colonization]].

O'Neill began researching high-energy [[particle physics]] at [[Princeton University|Princeton]] in 1954, after he received his doctorate from [[Cornell University]]. Two years later, he published his theory for a particle storage ring. This invention allowed [[particle accelerator]]s at much higher energies than had previously been possible. In 1965 at [[Stanford University]], he performed the first colliding beam physics experiment.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/>

While teaching physics at Princeton, O'Neill became interested in the possibility that humans could survive and live in outer space. He researched and proposed a futuristic idea for human settlement in space, the O'Neill cylinder, in "The Colonization of Space", his first paper on the subject. He held a conference on [[space manufacturing]] at Princeton in 1975. Many who became post-[[Apollo program|Apollo]]-era space activists attended. O'Neill built his first [[Mass Driver 1|mass driver prototype]] with professor [[Henry Kolm]] in 1976. He considered mass drivers critical for extracting the mineral resources of the [[Moon]] and [[asteroid]]s. His award-winning book ''[[The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space]]'' inspired a generation of space exploration advocates. He died of [[leukemia]] in 1992.

==Birth, education, and family life==
O'Neill was born in [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn, New York]], on February 6, 1927, to Edward Gerard O'Neill, a lawyer, and Dorothy Lewis O'Neill (née Kitchen).<ref name="GaleBio">[[#GaleBio|"Gerard K. O'Neill" ''Notable Scientists: From 1900 to the Present'']]</ref><ref name="GaleAuth">[[#GaleAuth|"Gerard K(itchen) O'Neill" ''Contemporary Authors Online'']]</ref><ref name="Rein77">{{harvnb|Rein|1977}}</ref> He had no siblings. His family moved to [[Speculator, New York]] when his father temporarily retired for health reasons.<ref name="Rein77"/> For high school, O'Neill attended [[Newburgh Free Academy]] in [[Newburgh, New York]]. While he was a student there he edited the school newspaper and took a job as a news broadcaster at a local radio station.<ref name="GaleBio"/> He graduated in 1944, during [[World War II]], and enlisted in the [[United States Navy]] on his 17th birthday.<ref name="GaleBio"/><ref name="Daniels92">{{harvnb|Daniels|1992}}</ref> The Navy trained him as a radar technician, which sparked his interest in science.<ref name="GaleBio"/>

After he was honorably discharged in 1946, O'Neill studied physics and mathematics at [[Swarthmore College]].<ref name="Daniels92"/><ref name="Dyson93p97">{{harvnb|Dyson|1993|p=97}}</ref> As a child he had discussed the possibilities of humans in space with his parents, and in college he enjoyed working on rocket equations. However, he did not see space science as an option for a career path in physics, choosing instead to pursue high-energy physics.<ref name="Henson77p8">{{harvnb|Henson|1977|p=8}}</ref> He graduated with [[Phi Beta Kappa]] honors in 1950. O'Neill then pursued graduate studies at [[Cornell University]] with the help of an [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|Atomic Energy Commission]] fellowship, and was awarded a [[PhD]] in physics in 1954.<ref name="Daniels92"/>

O'Neill married Sylvia Turlington, also a Swarthmore graduate, in June 1950.<ref name="GaleBio"/><ref name="Turlington50">[[#Turlington50|"Sylvia Turlington Wed at Her Home" ''New York Times'']]</ref> They had a son, Roger, and two daughters, Janet and Eleanor, before their marriage ended in divorce in 1966.<ref name="GaleBio"/><ref name="Rein77"/>

One of O'Neill's favorite activities was flying. He held instrument certifications in both powered and [[Glider (sailplane)|sailplane]] flight and held the [[FAI Gliding Commission|FAI]] Diamond Badge, a gliding award.<ref name="Rein77"/><ref>[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], back matter</ref> During his first cross-country glider flight in April 1973, he was assisted on the ground by Renate "Tasha" Steffen. He had met Tasha, who was 21 years younger than him, previously through the [[YMCA]] International Club. They were married the day after his flight.<ref name="GaleAuth"/><ref name="Rein77"/> They had a son, Edward O'Neill.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.towntopics.com/may2808/obits.html |title=''Town Topics'', Princeton local newspaper |access-date=April 8, 2009 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304031718/http://www.towntopics.com/may2808/obits.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

==High-energy physics research==
After graduating from Cornell, O'Neill accepted a position as an instructor at [[Princeton University]].<ref name="Daniels92"/> There he started his research into high-energy [[particle physics]]. In 1956, his second year of teaching, he published a two-page article that theorized that the particles produced by a [[particle accelerator]] could be stored for a few seconds in a [[storage ring]].<ref name="physrev-sr">{{Cite journal|last1=O'Neill |first1=G. |author-link1=Gerard K. O'Neill |title=Storage-Ring Synchrotron: Device for High-Energy Physics Research |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.102.1418 |journal=[[Physical Review]] |volume=102 |issue=5 |pages=1418–1419 |year=1956 |bibcode=1956PhRv..102.1418O |url=http://www.feynman.princeton.edu/mumu/physics/oneill_pr_102_1418_56.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306163409/http://www.feynman.princeton.edu/mumu/physics/oneill_pr_102_1418_56.pdf |archive-date=March 6, 2012 }}</ref> The stored particles could then be directed to collide with another [[particle beam]]. This would increase the energy of the particle collision over the previous method, which directed the beam at a fixed target.<ref name="Dyson93p98">{{harvnb|Dyson|1993|p=98}}</ref> His ideas were not immediately accepted by the physics community.<ref name="GaleBio"/>

O'Neill became an assistant professor at Princeton in 1956, and was promoted to associate professor in 1959.<ref name="GaleBio"/><ref name="GaleAuth"/> He visited Stanford University in 1957 to meet with [[Wolfgang K. H. Panofsky]].<ref>{{harvnb|Hoddeson|1997|p=265}} {{blockquote|O'Neill visited HEPL in 1957 to discuss colliding beams with Wolfgang K. H. Panofsky, then the director of that laboratory, and to seek collaborators.}}</ref> This resulted in a collaboration between Princeton and Stanford to build the {{ill|Colliding Beam Experiment|ru|CBX}} (CBX).<ref>{{harvnb|Richter|2002}} {{blockquote|This facility, first proposed by Gerard K. O’Neill of Princeton, and built at the High-Energy Physics Lab by a Princeton-Stanford collaboration, is the grandfather of all electron colliding-beam machines.}}</ref> With a US$800,000 grant from the [[Office of Naval Research]], construction of the first particle storage rings began in 1958 at the Stanford High-Energy Physics Laboratory.<ref>{{harvnb|Hoddeson|1997|p=267}} {{blockquote|The Office of Naval Research, a very imaginative organization that was then the principal supporter of fundamental research in physics, funded the project to the tune of $800,000, thanks to the persuasive powers of Panofsky.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Richter|2002}} {{blockquote|The construction of the first serious colliding-beam system began there in 1958 ...}}</ref> He figured out how to capture the particles and, by pumping the air out to produce a [[vacuum]], store them long enough to experiment on them.<ref>{{harvnb|Dyson|1993|pp=97–98}} {{blockquote|He solved the tough technical problems of injecting a beam from an accelerator into the ring and keeping the betatron oscillations of the particles in the ring small, so that a substantial fraction of the injected particles were stably captured.}}</ref><ref>[[#GaleBio|"Gerard K. O'Neill" ''Notable Scientists: From 1900 to the Present'']] {{blockquote|Finally obtaining financial support in 1959 from the Office of Naval Research and the Atomic Energy Commission, O'Neill and his colleagues built two particle storage rings at Stanford University that used his high-vacuum technique and successfully demonstrated his colliding-beam theory.}}</ref> CBX stored its first beam on March 28, 1962. O'Neill became a full professor of physics in 1965.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/>

In collaboration with [[Burton Richter]], O'Neill performed the first colliding beam physics experiment in 1965. In this experiment, electron beams from the Mark III linear accelerator at the Stanford High-Energy Physics Laboratory (HEPL) were collected in the two CBX storage rings and then directed to collide at an energy of 600 [[Electron volt|MeV]]. The results proved that the charge of an electron is contained in a volume less than 100 [[Metre#SI prefixed forms of metre|attometers]] across. O'Neill considered his device to be capable of only seconds of storage, but, by creating an even stronger vacuum, others were able to increase this to hours.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/> In 1979, he, with physicist David C. Cheng, wrote the graduate-level textbook ''Elementary Particle Physics: An Introduction''.<ref name="GaleAuth"/> He retired from teaching in 1985, but remained associated with Princeton as ''professor emeritus'' until his death.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/>

==Space colonization==
{{Main|Space colonization}}

===Origin of the idea (1969)===
[[Image:S88 33646.jpg|thumb|[[NASA]] envisioned an ambitious scientific exploration of the [[Moon]].]]
O'Neill saw great potential in the United States space program, especially the [[Apollo program|Apollo missions]]. He applied to the Astronaut Corps after NASA opened it up to civilian scientists in 1966. Later, when asked why he wanted to go on the Moon missions, he said, "to be alive now and not take part in it seemed terribly myopic".<ref name="Rein77"/> He was put through NASA's rigorous mental and physical examinations. During this time he met [[Brian O'Leary]], also a scientist-astronaut candidate, who became his good friend.<ref name="ONeill77p243">[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], p. 243</ref> O'Leary was selected for [[Astronaut Group 6]] but O'Neill was not.<ref>[[#JSCBio|Astronaut Biographies: Former Astronauts]]</ref>

O'Neill became interested in the idea of space colonization in 1969 while he was teaching freshman physics at Princeton University.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/><ref name="CoEvInt">{{harvnb|Brand|1977}}</ref> His students were growing cynical about the benefits of science to humanity because of the controversy surrounding the [[Vietnam War]].<ref name="ONeill77p233">[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], p. 233</ref><ref name="Overend77">{{harvnb|Overend|1977}}</ref> To give them something relevant to study, he began using examples from the Apollo program as applications of elementary physics.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/><ref name="Rein77"/> O'Neill posed the question during an extra seminar he gave to a few of his students: "Is the surface of a planet really the right place for an expanding technological civilization?"<ref name="CoEvInt"/> His students' research convinced him that the answer was no.<ref name="CoEvInt"/>

[[Image:Bernal Sphere 3.jpeg|thumb|left|[[Bernal sphere]], an "inside-out planet"]]

O'Neill was inspired by the papers written by his students. He began to work out the details of a program to build self-supporting space habitats in free space.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/><ref name="Daniels92"/> Among the details was how to provide the inhabitants of a space colony with an Earth-like environment. His students had designed giant pressurized structures, spun up to approximate Earth gravity by [[centrifugal force]]. With the population of the colony living on the inner surface of a sphere or cylinder, these structures resembled "inside-out planets". He found that pairing counter-rotating cylinders would eliminate the need to spin them using rockets.<ref name="CoEvInt"/> This configuration has since been known as the ''[[O'Neill cylinder]]''.

===First paper (1970–1974)===
Looking for an outlet for his ideas, O'Neill wrote a paper titled "The Colonization of Space", and for four years attempted to have it published.<ref>{{harvnb|Brand|1977}} {{blockquote|O'Neill: So then it went through a period of-let's see, that was 1970, and it was not until four more years that I was able to get an article published.}}</ref> He submitted it to several journals and magazines, including ''Scientific American'' and ''Science'', only to have it rejected by the reviewers. During this time O'Neill gave lectures on space colonization at [[Hampshire College]], Princeton, and other schools. The Hampshire lecture was facilitated by O'Leary, by now an assistant professor of astronomy and science policy assessment at the institution; in 1976, he joined O'Neill's research group at Princeton.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://space.nss.org/just-like-starting-over-olearys-startling-new-direction/ |title='Just Like Starting Over': O'Leary's Startling New Direction|author=Emily Carney|date=September 21, 2019 |access-date=May 28, 2020 |archive-date=September 29, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200929041419/https://space.nss.org/just-like-starting-over-olearys-startling-new-direction/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Many students and staff attending the lectures became enthusiastic about the possibility of living in space.<ref name="CoEvInt"/> Another outlet for O'Neill to explore his ideas was with his children; on walks in the forest they speculated about life in a space colony.<ref>{{harvnb|Brand|1977}} {{blockquote|O'Neill: ... I used to talk about it to my children. I'd take them on walks in the woods, and speculate about what life in a space colony would be like....}}</ref> His paper finally appeared in the September 1974 issue of ''[[Physics Today]]''. In it, he argued that building space colonies would solve several important problems: {{cquote|It is important to realize the enormous power of the space-colonization technique. If we begin to use it soon enough, and if we employ it wisely, at least five of the most serious problems now facing the world can be solved without recourse to repression: bringing every human being up to a living standard now enjoyed only by the most fortunate; protecting the biosphere from damage caused by transportation and industrial pollution; finding high quality living space for a world population that is doubling every 35 years; finding clean, practical energy sources; preventing overload of Earth's heat balance.|Gerard K. O'Neill|"The Colonization of Space"<ref name="ONeill74">[[#ONeill74|O'Neill 1974]]</ref>}}

[[Image:Lagrange 2 mass.gif|thumb|right|Diagram of the Lagrange points in the Earth-Moon system]]

He explored the possibilities of flying gliders inside a space colony, finding that the enormous volume could support atmospheric thermals.<ref>[[#ONeill74|O'Neill 1974]] {{cquote|As an enthusiastic glider pilot, I have checked the question of thermal scales: the soaring pilots of the colonial age should find sufficient atmospheric instability to provide them with lift.}}</ref> He calculated that humanity could expand on this man-made frontier to 20,000 times its population.<ref>[[#ONeill74|O'Neill 1974]] {{blockquote|the ultimate size limit for the human race on the newly available frontier is at least 20,000 times its present value.}}</ref> The initial colonies would be built at the Earth-Moon {{L4}} and {{L5}} [[Lagrangian point|Lagrange points]].<ref>[[#ONeill74|O'Neill 1974]] {{blockquote|For the first colony it is probably best to choose a particular point on that sphere, within easy range of both Earth and Moon, not so close as to be eclipsed often, and preferably stable against displacements in all three coordinates. The {{L4}} and {{L5}} Lagrange libration points satisfy all these conditions.}}</ref> {{L4}} and {{L5}} are stable points in the [[Solar System]] where a spacecraft can maintain its position without expending energy. The paper was well received, but many who would begin work on the project had already been introduced to his ideas before it was even published.<ref name="CoEvInt"/> The paper received a few critical responses. Some questioned the practicality of lifting tens of thousands of people into orbit and his estimates for the production output of initial colonies.<ref name="ONeill77p253">[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], p. 253</ref>

While he was waiting for his paper to be published, O'Neill organized a small two-day conference in May 1974 at Princeton to discuss the possibility of colonizing outer space.<ref name="CoEvInt"/> The conference, titled ''First Conference on Space Colonization'', was funded by [[Stewart Brand]]'s [[Point Foundation (environment)|Point Foundation]] and Princeton University.<ref name="ONeill77p249">[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], p. 249</ref> Among those who attended were [[Eric Drexler]] (at the time a freshman at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]]), scientist-astronaut [[Joseph P. Allen|Joe Allen]] (from Astronaut Group 6), [[Freeman Dyson]], and science reporter [[Walter S. Sullivan|Walter Sullivan]].<ref name="CoEvInt"/> Representatives from NASA also attended and brought estimates of launch costs expected on the planned [[Space Shuttle program|Space Shuttle]].<ref name="CoEvInt"/> O'Neill thought of the attendees as "a band of daring radicals".<ref name="Henson77p10">{{harvnb|Henson|1977|p=10}}</ref> Sullivan's article on the conference was published on the front page of ''[[The New York Times]]'' on May 13, 1974.<ref>{{harvnb|Sullivan|1974}}</ref> As media coverage grew, O'Neill was inundated with letters from people who were excited about living in space.<ref>[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], pp. 250–252</ref> To stay in touch with them, O'Neill began keeping a mailing list and started sending out updates on his progress.<ref name="CoEvInt"/><ref name="ONeill77p252">[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], p. 252</ref> A few months later he heard [[Peter Glaser]] speak about [[solar power satellite]]s at NASA's [[Goddard Space Flight Center]]. O'Neill realized that, by building these satellites, his space colonies could quickly recover the cost of their construction.<ref name="ONeill77p255">[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], p. 255</ref> According to O'Neill, "the profound difference between this and everything else done in space is the potential of generating large amounts of new wealth".<ref name="Rein77"/>

===NASA studies (1975–1977)===
O'Neill held a much larger conference the following May titled ''Princeton University Conference on Space Manufacturing''.<ref name="ONeill77p256">[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], p. 256</ref> At this conference more than two dozen speakers presented papers, including [[Keith Henson|Keith]] and [[Carolyn Meinel|Carolyn Henson]] from [[Tucson, Arizona]].<ref name="Erichsen94">{{harvnb|Erichsen|1994}}</ref><ref name="AIAA75">[[#AIAA75|''Space Manufacturing Facilities'' 1977]]</ref>

After the conference Carolyn Henson arranged a meeting between O'Neill and Arizona Congressman [[Mo Udall]], then a leading contender for the [[Democratic Party presidential primaries, 1976|1976 Democratic presidential nomination]]. Udall wrote a letter of support, which he asked the Hensons to publicize, for O'Neill's work.<ref name="Erichsen94"/> The Hensons included his letter in the first issue of the [[L5 Society|L-5 Society]] newsletter, sent to everyone on O'Neill's mailing list and those who had signed up at the conference.<ref name="Erichsen94"/><ref>{{harvnb|Udall|1975}}</ref>

[[Image:ONeillSenate1976.gif|thumb|left|O'Neill testifying before the Senate Subcommittee on January 19, 1976]]

In June 1975, O'Neill led a ten-week study of permanent space habitats at NASA Ames. During the study he was called away to testify on July 23 to the [[United States House of Representatives|House]] Subcommittee on Space Science and Applications.<ref name="ONeill77p282">[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], p. 282</ref> On January 19, 1976, he also appeared before the [[United States Senate|Senate]] Subcommittee on Aerospace Technology and National Needs. In a presentation titled ''Solar Power from Satellites'', he laid out his case for an Apollo-style program for building power plants in space.<ref name="ONeill77p264">[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], p. 264</ref> He returned to Ames in June 1976 and 1977 to lead studies on space manufacturing.<ref name="SSIHistory">[[#SSIHistory|''SSI History'']]</ref> In these studies, NASA developed detailed plans to establish bases on the Moon where space-suited workers would mine the mineral resources needed to build space colonies and solar power satellites.<ref name="ONeillAmes77">[[#ONeillAmes77|O'Neill ''Summer Study Notes'' 1977]]</ref>

===Private funding (1977–1978)===
Although NASA was supporting his work with grants of up to $500,000 per year, O'Neill became frustrated by the bureaucracy and politics inherent in government-funded research.<ref name="GaleBio"/><ref name="Overend77"/> He thought that small privately funded groups could develop [[space technology]] faster than government agencies.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/> In 1977, O'Neill and his wife Tasha founded the [[Space Studies Institute]], a non-profit organization, at Princeton University.<ref name="Daniels92"/><ref>[[#GaleBio|"Gerard K. O'Neill" ''Notable Scientists: From 1900 to the Present'']] {{blockquote|Therefore, in 1977, he sought and obtained private support for a new, non-profit corporation called the Space Studies Institute. Located at Princeton University, the Space Studies Institute supports technical research on the science and engineering of living and working in space with grants made possible by members' contributions.}}</ref> SSI received initial funding of almost $100,000 from private donors, and in early 1978 began to support basic research into technologies needed for space manufacturing and settlement.<ref>[[#SSIHistory|''SSI History'']] {{blockquote|At the end of the year and with legal matters attended to, SSI was given a strong head-start by two gifts from private donors, totaling nearly $100,000.}}</ref>

[[Image:ONEILLMASS.GIF|thumb|right|[[Henry Kolm|Kolm]] (left) and O'Neill (center) with a [[mass driver]]]]
One of [[Space Studies Institute|SSI's]] first grants funded the development of the [[mass driver]], a device first proposed by O'Neill in 1974.<ref name="AboutSSI">[[#AboutSSI|''About SSI'']]</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Kolm|1992|p=123}} {{blockquote|An offshoot of this maglev research resulted in the concept of the mass driver by Professor Gerard K. O'Neill of Princeton University in 1974.}}</ref> Mass drivers are based on the [[coilgun]] design, adapted to accelerate a non-magnetic object.<ref>{{harvnb|Meinel|2007}} {{blockquote|Someone in NASA apparently agreed, because in 1976 the space agency awarded a $50 000 contract to O'Neill and MIT professor Henry Kolm, part of which they used to build a coilgun. Called the Mass Driver I, the 8-meter-long device had its public debut at Princeton, in the lobby of Chadwin Hall, where a conference on space colonies was taking place.}}</ref> One application O'Neill proposed for mass drivers was to throw baseball-sized chunks of ore mined from the surface of the Moon into space.<ref name="Weintraub84p304">{{harvnb|Weintraub|1984|p=304}}</ref><ref name="COMPUTE"/> Once in space, the ore could be used as raw material for building space colonies and solar power satellites. He took a sabbatical from Princeton to work on mass drivers at MIT. There he served as the [[Jerome C. Hunsaker Visiting Professor of Aerospace Systems|Hunsaker Visiting Professor of Aerospace]] during the 1976–77 academic year.<ref>{{harvnb|Kolm|1992|p=123}}</ref> At MIT, he, [[Henry Kolm|Henry H. Kolm]], and a group of student volunteers built their [[Mass Driver 1|first mass driver prototype]].<ref name="Henson77p10"/><ref name="SSIHistory"/><ref name="AboutSSI"/> The eight-foot (2.5&nbsp;m) long prototype could apply 33&nbsp;''[[g-force|g]]'' (320&nbsp;m/s<sup>2</sup>) of acceleration to an object inserted into it.<ref name="Henson77p10"/><ref name="SSIHistory"/><ref name="Weintraub84p304"/> With financial assistance from SSI, later prototypes improved this to 1,800&nbsp;''g'' (18,000&nbsp;m/s<sup>2</sup>), enough acceleration that a mass driver only 520 feet (160&nbsp;m) long could launch material off the surface of the Moon.<ref name="SSIHistory"/>

===Opposition (1977–1985)===
In 1977, O'Neill saw the peak of interest in space colonization, along with the publication of his first book, ''[[The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space|The High Frontier]]''.<ref name="Erichsen94"/> He and his wife were flying between meetings, interviews, and hearings.<ref name="Rein77"/> On October 9, the [[CBS]] program ''[[60 Minutes]]'' ran a segment about space colonies. Later they aired responses from the viewers, which included one from Senator [[William Proxmire]], chairman of the Senate Subcommittee responsible for NASA's budget and an aggressive critic of [[government failure]]. His response was: "It's the best argument yet for chopping NASA's funding to the bone .... I say not a penny for this nutty fantasy".<ref>{{harvnb|Lovell|1977}} {{blockquote|"It's the best argument yet for chopping NASA's funding to the bone. As Chairman of the Senate Subcommittee responsible for NASA's appropriations, I say not a penny for this nutty fantasy..."}}</ref> He successfully eliminated spending on space colonization research from the budget.<ref>{{harvnb|Proxmire|1978}}</ref> In 1978, [[Paul Werbos]] wrote for the L-5 newsletter, "no one expects Congress to commit us to O'Neill's concept of large-scale space habitats; people in NASA are almost paranoid about the public relations aspects of the idea".<ref>{{harvnb|Werbos|1978|p=15}}</ref> When it became clear that a government-funded colonization effort was politically impossible, popular support for O'Neill's ideas started to evaporate.<ref name="Erichsen94"/>

Other pressures on O'Neill's colonization plan were the high cost of access to Earth orbit and the declining cost of energy. Building solar power stations in space was economically attractive when energy prices spiked during the [[1979 energy crisis|1979 oil crisis]]. When prices dropped in the early 1980s, funding for space solar power research dried up.<ref>{{harvnb|Davis|2006}}</ref> His plan had also been based on NASA's estimates for the flight rate and launch cost of the Space Shuttle, numbers that turned out to have been wildly optimistic. His 1977 book quoted a Space Shuttle launch cost of $10 million, but in 1981 the subsidized price given to commercial customers started at $38 million.<ref name="ONeill77p134">[[#ONeill77|O'Neill ''The High Frontier'' 1977]], p. 134</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Hanushek|1985|p=2}}</ref> A 1985 accounting of the full cost of a launch in 1985 raised this as high as $180 million per flight.<ref>{{harvnb|Hanushek|1985|p=6}} (in 1982 dollars)</ref>

O'Neill was appointed by United States President [[Ronald Reagan]] to the National Commission on Space in 1985.<ref name="Daniels92"/> The commission, led by former NASA administrator [[Thomas O. Paine|Thomas Paine]], proposed that the government commit to opening the inner Solar System for human settlement within 50 years.<ref name="Paine86">{{harvnb|Paine|1986}}</ref> Their report was released in May 1986, four months after the [[Space Shuttle Challenger]] broke up on ascent.<ref name="Paine86"/>

==Writing career==
[[Image:Spacecolony1.jpg|thumb|right|O'Neill cylinders as illustrated in [[The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space|''The High Frontier'']]]]

O'Neill's popular science book ''[[The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space]]'' (1977) combined fictional accounts of space settlers with an explanation of his plan to build space colonies. Its publication established him as the spokesman for the space colonization movement.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/> It won the [[Phi Beta Kappa Award in Science]] that year, and prompted Swarthmore College to grant him an [[Honorary degree|honorary doctorate]].<ref name="GaleAuth"/><ref name="PBKAwards">[[#PBKAwards|''Phi Beta Kappa Award in Science Winners'']]</ref> ''The High Frontier'' has been translated into five languages and remained in print as of 2008.<ref name="SSIHistory"/>

His 1981 book ''[[2081: A Hopeful View of the Human Future]]'' was an exercise in [[futures studies|futurology]]. O'Neill narrated it as a visitor to Earth from a space colony beyond Pluto.<ref>{{harvnb|Ferris|1981}}</ref> The book explored the effects of technologies he called "drivers of change" on the coming century. Some technologies he described were [[Space colonization|space colonies]], [[Space-based solar power|solar power satellites]], [[anti-aging]] drugs, [[Hydrogen vehicle|hydrogen-propelled cars]], [[Weather modification|climate control]], and underground [[Maglev train|magnetic trains]]. He left the social structure of the 1980s intact, assuming that humanity would remain unchanged even as it expanded into the Solar System. Reviews of ''2081'' were mixed. ''New York Times'' reviewer [[John Noble Wilford]] found the book "imagination-stirring", but [[Charles Nicol]] thought the technologies described were unacceptably far-fetched.<ref name="GaleAuth"/>

In his book ''The Technology Edge'', published in 1983, O'Neill wrote about economic competition with Japan.<ref name="Weil84">{{harvnb|Weil|1984}}</ref> He argued that the United States had to develop six industries to compete: [[Microfabrication|microengineering]], [[robotics]], [[genetic engineering]], [[Magnetic levitation|magnetic flight]], [[Flying car (fiction)|family aircraft]], and [[Outline of space science|space science.]]<ref name="COMPUTE">{{harvnb|Bateman|1984}}</ref> He also thought that industrial development was suffering from short-sighted executives, self-interested unions, high taxes, and poor education of Americans. According to reviewer Henry Weil, O'Neill's detailed explanations of [[emerging technologies]] differentiated the book from others on the subject.<ref name="Weil84"/>

==Entrepreneurial efforts==
[[Image:RDSS Diagram.png|thumb|Design for the satellite position determination system]]

O'Neill founded Geostar Corporation to develop a satellite position determination system for which he was granted a patent in 1982.<ref>[[#GaleBio|"Gerard K. O'Neill" ''Notable Scientists: From 1900 to the Present'']] {{blockquote|In 1983, he founded the Geostar Corporation which, based on O'Neill's own patent, developed the first private satellite navigational system to guide travel on earth.}}</ref> The system, primarily intended to track aircraft, was called Radio Determination Satellite Service (RDSS).<ref name="COMPUTE"/> In April 1983 Geostar applied to the FCC for a license to broadcast from three satellites, which would cover the entire United States. Geostar launched GSTAR-2 into [[geosynchronous orbit]] in 1986. Its [[transmitter]] package permanently failed two months later, so Geostar began tests of RDSS by transmitting from other satellites.<ref>{{harvnb|Martin|2000|pp=263–264}} {{blockquote|In 1987 ... the Geostar Corporation began providing limited one-way position determination service (Geostar System 1.0) from mobile subscribers, primarily in the long-distance trucking industry, using the French Argos transponders on U.S. meteorological satellites.}} {{blockquote|The second was on GStar 2, launched in 1986; the subsystem operated properly in initial testing but failed less than two months after launch.}}</ref> With his health failing, O'Neill became less involved with the company at the same time it started to run into trouble.<ref name="SmitGeo">[[#SmitGeo|''Geostar Corporation Records 1983–1991'']]</ref> In February 1991 Geostar filed for bankruptcy and its licenses were sold to [[Motorola]] for the [[Iridium satellite constellation]] project.<ref>[[#Sat91|''Satellite News'' 1991]] {{blockquote|Satellite News has learned that Iridium Inc., a Motorola affiliate, and Comsat Corp. have purchased the assets of ill-fated, Washington, D.C.-based Geostar Corp. at a bankruptcy auction proceeding late last week.}}</ref> Although the system was eventually replaced by [[Global Positioning System|GPS]], O'Neill made significant advances in the field of position determination.<ref name="SmitGeo"/>

O'Neill founded O'Neill Communications in Princeton in 1986. He introduced his Local Area Wireless Networking, or LAWN, system at the PC Expo in New York in 1989.<ref name="PCExLAWN">{{harvnb|Sexton|1989}}</ref> The LAWN system allowed two computers to exchange messages over a range of a couple hundred feet at a cost of about $500 per node.<ref name="PerCompLAWN">{{harvnb|Honan|1990}}</ref> O'Neill Communications went out of business in 1993; the LAWN technology was sold to Omnispread Communications. As of 2008, Omnispread continued to sell a variant of O'Neill's LAWN system.<ref name="Keystone06p4">[[#Keystone06|Keystone press release 2006]], p. 4</ref>

On November 18, 1991, O'Neill filed a patent application for a [[vactrain]] system.<ref>{{cite patent|country=US|number=5282424|pubdate=1994-02-01|title=High speed transport system|inventor1-last=O'Neill|inventor1-first=Gerard K.}}</ref> He called the company he wanted to form ''VSE International'', for velocity, silence, and efficiency.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/>  However, the concept itself he called ''[[Magnetic Flight]]''.  The vehicles, instead of running on a pair of tracks, would be elevated using electromagnetic force by a single track within a tube (permanent magnets in the track, with variable magnets on the vehicle), and propelled by electromagnetic forces through tunnels. He estimated the trains could reach speeds of up to 2,500&nbsp;mph (4,000&nbsp;km/h)—about five times faster than a jet airliner—if the air was evacuated from the tunnels.<ref name="Daniels92"/> To obtain such speeds, the vehicle would accelerate for the first half of the trip, and then decelerate for the second half of the trip. The acceleration was planned to be a maximum of about one-half of the force of gravity. O'Neill planned to build a network of stations connected by these tunnels, but he died two years before his first patent on it was granted.<ref name="Dyson93p98"/>

==Death and legacy==
[[Image:Pegasus Air Launch.jpg|thumb|O'Neill's ashes were carried on the upper stage of an [[Pegasus (rocket)|Orbital Sciences Pegasus]]]]

O'Neill was diagnosed with [[leukemia]] in 1985.<ref name="SmitGeo"/> He died on April 27, 1992, from complications of the disease at the [[Sequoia Hospital]] in [[Redwood City, California]].<!-- Here he's back in Redwood City, next door to Stanford, yet he remained affiliated with Princeton ... confused if he moved to Stanford duirng his career or what ?  --><ref name="Daniels92"/><ref name="Dyson93p97"/> He was survived by his wife Tasha, his ex-wife Sylvia, and his four children.<ref name="Daniels92"/><ref>[[#Roger08|"O'Neill, Dr. Roger A." 2008]]</ref> A sample of his incinerated remains was [[Space burial|buried in space]].<ref name="Simons97">{{harvnb|Simons|1997}}</ref> The [[Celestis]] vial containing his ashes was attached with vials of other Celestis participants to a [[Pegasus (rocket)|Pegasus XL]] rocket and launched into Earth orbit on April 21, 1997.<ref name="Simons97"/><ref>[[#FAA1997|''Quarterly Launch Report'' 3Q 1997]]</ref> It re-entered the atmosphere in May 2002.<ref>[[#Debris02|"Pegasus HAPS Rocket Body Reentry Prediction" 2002]]</ref>

O'Neill directed his Space Studies Institute to continue their efforts "until people are living and working in space".<ref>[[#SSIHistory|''SSI History'']] {{blockquote|At the last board meeting that he attended, one month before he succumbed to a seven-year bout with leukemia, Dr. Gerard O'Neill firmly stated, "Our mission is not complete until people are living and working in space."}}</ref> After his death, management of SSI was passed to his son Roger and colleague Freeman Dyson.<ref name="SSIHistory"/> SSI continued to hold conferences every other year to bring together scientists studying space colonization until 2001.<ref>{{harvnb|Hoyt|2006|p=20}} {{blockquote|The conference was held again at Princeton the following year in cooperation with the [[American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics]], and took place every other year from 1975 to 2001.}}</ref>

O'Neill's work informs the company [[Blue Origin]] founded by [[Jeff Bezos]], which wants to build the infrastructure for future space colonization.<ref>{{Cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/05/09/science/jeff-bezos-moon.html| title=Jeff Bezos Unveils Blue Origin's Vision for Space, and a Moon Lander| newspaper=The New York Times| date=May 9, 2019| last1=Chang| first1=Kenneth| access-date=May 30, 2019| archive-date=May 10, 2019| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190510110122/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/05/09/science/jeff-bezos-moon.html| url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Henry Kolm]] went on to start Magplane Technology in the 1990s to develop the magnetic transportation technology that O'Neill had written about. In 2007, Magplane demonstrated a working magnetic pipeline system to transport phosphate ore in Florida. The system ran at a speed of 40&nbsp;mph (65&nbsp;km/h), far slower than the high-speed trains O'Neill envisioned.<ref>{{harvnb|Dickson|2007}} {{blockquote|The Magplane Pipeline Technology was demonstrated in Florida at IMC Global Inc., which has merged with Cargill Crop Nutrition to form The Mosaic Company [NOS-NY]—the world's leading producer of potash and phosphate crop nutrients. In the demonstration, phosphate ore was successfully transported at speeds up to 65 kilometers/hour using the pipeline system that utilized rare earth (neodymium-iron-boron) permanent magnets on the capsules over a 275-metre long pipeline containing a linear synchronous motor winding.}}</ref><ref>[[#MTIPrincipals|''MTI Principals'']]</ref>

All three of the founders of the [[Space Frontier Foundation]], an organization dedicated to opening the space frontier to human settlement, were supporters of O'Neill's ideas and had worked with him in various capacities at the Space Studies Institute.<ref>{{harvnb|Tumlinson|2006}}</ref>  One of them, [[Rick Tumlinson]], describes three men as models for space advocacy: [[Wernher von Braun]], Gerard K. O'Neill, and [[Carl Sagan]]. Von Braun pushed for "projects that ordinary people can be proud of but not participate in".<ref name="Grierson04">{{harvnb|Grierson|2004}}</ref> Sagan wanted to explore the universe from a distance. O'Neill, with his grand scheme for settlement of the Solar System, emphasized moving ordinary people off the Earth "en masse".<ref name="Grierson04"/>

The [[National Space Society]] (NSS) gives the Gerard K. O'Neill Memorial Award for Space Settlement Advocacy to individuals noted for their contributions in the area of space settlement. Their contributions can be scientific, legislative, and educational. The award is a trophy cast in the shape of a [[Bernal sphere]]. The NSS first bestowed the award in 2007 on lunar entrepreneur and former astronaut [[Harrison Schmitt]]. In 2008, it was given to physicist [[John Marburger]].<ref name="NSSAward">[[#NSSAward|NSS Gerard K. O'Neill Memorial Award]]</ref>

As of November, 2013, Gerard O'Neill's papers and work are now located in the archives at the [[Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum]], [[Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nss.org/dr-gerard-k-oneills-collection-underscores-his-continuing-relevance-intensity/|title=Dr. Gerard K. O’Neill’s Collection Underscores His Continuing Relevance, Intensity |website=Nww.org|date=May 2, 2023|access-date=July 9, 2026}}</ref>

==Patents==
O'Neill was granted six patents in total (two posthumously) in the areas of global position determination and magnetic levitation.
* {{Cite patent|country=US|number=4359733}} Satellite-based vehicle position determining system, granted November 16, 1982
* {{Cite patent|country=US|number=4744083}} Satellite-based position determining and message transfer system with monitoring of link quality, granted May 10, 1988
* {{Cite patent|country=US|number=4839656}} Position determination and message transfer system employing satellites and stored terrain map, granted June 13, 1989
* {{Cite patent|country=US|number=4965586}} Position determination and message transfer system employing satellites and stored terrain map, granted October 23, 1990
* {{Cite patent|country=US|number=5282424}} High speed transport system, granted February 1, 1994
* {{Cite patent|country=US|number=5433155}} High speed transport system, granted July 18, 1995
